topics.title: Network Vulnerabilities and Attacks
topics.hook: Every laptop on a school network suddenly sends its traffic through one student's machine before reaching the router. Nobody touched a cable. How?
concept: Local networks trust by default. ARP maps IP addresses to MAC (hardware) addresses; ARP poisoning sends forged replies so victims map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC, putting the attacker on-path (man-in-the-middle) to sniff or alter traffic. MAC spoofing fakes a hardware address to impersonate a device or bypass MAC filters. MAC flooding overwhelms a switch's address table so it broadcasts traffic everywhere, enabling eavesdropping.

DNS poisoning corrupts name-to-IP lookups so users typing a real domain land on an attacker's server, often for credential harvesting. Denial of service (DoS) floods a target from one source; distributed DoS (DDoS) uses many. A smurf attack sends ICMP echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed IP, so every host replies to the victim at once.

Wireless adds rogue access points (unauthorized APs plugged into the network) and beacon frames, the packets an AP broadcasts to announce its SSID, which attackers can spoof. Automated vulnerability scanners help defenders find these weaknesses first.
terms: Forged ARP messages linking an attacker's MAC to another device's IP.
Attacker positioned between two parties, intercepting or altering traffic (formerly man-in-the-middle).
Changing a device's reported MAC address to impersonate another.
Overloading a switch's MAC table so it forwards frames to all ports.
Corrupting DNS records or caches to redirect users.
ICMP broadcast amplification against a spoofed victim IP.
Denial of service from many distributed sources.
An unauthorized wireless AP connected to a network.
Wireless packet advertising an AP's SSID and capabilities.
traps: ARP works at the local network level. ARP poisoning can't directly target a host across the internet.
Smurf uses ICMP and broadcast amplification; don't confuse it with a generic SYN flood.

items.stem: An attacker sends forged replies so hosts associate the default gateway's IP with the attacker's MAC address. Which attack is this?
items.why: Forging the IP-to-MAC mapping is ARP poisoning.

items.stem: Why does MAC flooding help an attacker eavesdrop on a switched network?
opts: A full MAC table can make the switch forward frames out every port
items.why: Without a usable table, the switch behaves like a hub, exposing traffic.

items.stem: Users typing their bank's correct domain are sent to a look-alike site. The URL in the address bar is correct. Which attack is MOST likely?
items.why: Correct name, wrong IP means name resolution was corrupted.

items.stem: A victim's server is overwhelmed by ICMP echo replies from hundreds of hosts after someone sends pings to a broadcast address with the victim's IP as the source. This is:
items.why: ICMP broadcast amplification with a spoofed source is a smurf attack.

items.stem: Thousands of compromised IoT devices flood a website with requests. This is BEST described as:
items.why: Many distributed sources flooding a target is DDoS.

items.stem: A network uses MAC filtering to allow only known devices. How might an attacker bypass it?
opts: Spoof the MAC address of an allowed device
items.why: MAC addresses are easy to observe and fake.

items.stem: An employee plugs a personal wireless router into an office network jack. Why is this HIGH risk?
opts: It creates a rogue access point that bypasses network security controls
Routers cannot connect to office jacks
items.why: An unmanaged AP gives outsiders a path inside, bypassing controls.

items.stem: A vulnerability scan finds the guest Wi-Fi and the finance network on the same flat network. How should this be documented?
opts: As a vulnerability that exposes finance systems to guests
items.why: Lack of separation is a documented weakness to address with segmentation.

topics.title: Protecting Networks: Managerial Controls and Wireless Security
topics.hook: You're handed a small office's Wi-Fi router. It's still using WEP, WPS is on, and the signal reaches the parking lot. What do you change first?
concept: Managerial controls set rules: router and switch configuration policies, VPN use policies, and wireless security policies define what is allowed and who approves changes. A VPN policy may forbid split tunneling, where some traffic goes through the VPN and some goes directly to the internet, because the direct path bypasses corporate protections.

Wireless security: use WPA3 (or WPA2 at minimum) with AES encryption. WEP is broken and should never be used. WPS (push-button or PIN pairing) is vulnerable to brute force and should be disabled. Enterprise networks use EAP with a central authentication server so each user has their own credentials instead of one shared password.

Other hardening: change default admin credentials, update firmware, reduce signal strength or aim antennas so coverage stays inside the building, and optionally disable SSID broadcast in beacon frames or use MAC filtering. Those last two are weak alone because SSIDs and MACs can still be discovered.
terms: Current Wi-Fi security standard with stronger encryption and protections.
Strong symmetric encryption used by WPA2/WPA3.
Simplified pairing feature vulnerable to PIN brute-force.
Framework for per-user authentication on enterprise Wi-Fi.
Sending only some traffic through a VPN, the rest directly.
Managerial rule defining approved device settings and change process.
traps: Hiding the SSID is not real security. Clients still reveal it when probing.
MAC filtering is easily bypassed with MAC spoofing.

items.stem: A router is configured with WEP. What is the BEST change?
opts: Keep WEP but use a longer key
items.why: WEP is broken; WPA3 with AES is the modern standard.

items.stem: Why should WPS be disabled on a business router?
opts: Its PIN can be brute-forced to gain network access
items.why: WPS PIN design makes it guessable.

items.stem: A company's VPN policy forbids split tunneling. What risk does this MOST directly reduce?
opts: Remote devices sending traffic to the internet outside corporate security controls
items.why: Full tunneling keeps all traffic under corporate inspection.

items.stem: A school wants each student's Wi-Fi login to be individually revocable. Which approach is BEST?
items.why: EAP ties access to individual accounts that can be disabled.

items.stem: Disabling SSID broadcast is a weak control mainly because:
opts: The SSID can still be discovered from client traffic
items.why: Clients probing for the network reveal its name.

items.stem: The office Wi-Fi is easily picked up in the public parking lot. Which configuration change BEST reduces this exposure?
opts: Lower AP transmit power and adjust placement/antenna direction
Change the SSID to a random name
items.why: Controlling signal reach limits who can attempt to connect.

items.stem: A written rule that all router configuration changes require approval and a change ticket is a:
items.why: Policies and procedures are managerial controls.

items.stem: Which set of wireless settings provides the STRONGEST layered protection?
opts: WPA3 + AES, WPS off, changed admin password, firmware updated
WPA2 + WPS on + default admin password
items.why: Strong encryption plus removal of known weak points is layered defense.

topics.title: Protecting Networks: Segmentation
topics.hook: A hospital's MRI machine, guest Wi-Fi, public website, and billing database are all on one network. An attacker gets into the guest Wi-Fi. What can they reach?
concept: Segmentation divides a network into zones so a compromise in one doesn't expose everything. It limits lateral movement and lets each zone have its own rules.

A screened subnet (DMZ) holds servers that must be reachable from the internet, such as a public web server, between an outer and inner firewall, so if one is compromised the internal network is still protected. Subnetting splits IP address ranges into smaller logical networks. VLANs (virtual LANs) separate traffic on the same physical switches into isolated groups, like guest, staff, and IoT.

Port security on switches restricts which MAC addresses can use a port and how many, limiting rogue devices and MAC flooding. Security zones group assets by trust level and data sensitivity, with traffic between zones filtered.
terms: Dividing a network into isolated parts to contain attacks.
Zone for public-facing servers, separated from the internal network.
Dividing an IP network into smaller address ranges.
Logical separation of devices on shared switch hardware.
Switch feature limiting which/how many MACs may use a port.
Group of assets with a shared trust level and access policy.
traps: A DMZ isn't 'outside' the security perimeter; it's a buffer zone with its own filtering.
VLANs separate traffic, but routing between VLANs still needs firewall rules to be secure.

items.stem: Where should a company place its public-facing web server?
opts: On the same subnet as the HR database
items.why: A DMZ isolates internet-facing servers from internal systems.

items.stem: Why does segmentation increase security?
opts: It limits how far an attacker can move after compromising one area
It removes the need for firewalls
items.why: Segments contain breaches and block lateral movement.

items.stem: A school wants smart boards, student devices, and staff computers isolated from each other on the same switches. Which technique fits BEST?
items.why: VLANs create logical separation over shared hardware.

items.stem: A switch is configured to allow only one specific MAC address on each office port. This is:
items.why: Restricting MACs per switch port is port security.

items.stem: Smart cameras with known weak firmware must stay on the network. Which is the BEST mitigation?
opts: Place them on an isolated IoT VLAN with tightly filtered access
Put them on the finance subnet
items.why: Isolating risky devices limits what a compromise can reach.

items.stem: An attacker compromises a guest Wi-Fi device on a network with NO segmentation. What is the MOST serious impact?
opts: They may reach internal servers directly
Nothing, because guest Wi-Fi is always isolated
items.why: A flat network lets the attacker reach everything.

items.stem: Dividing 10.0.0.0/16 into 10.0.1.0/24 for staff and 10.0.2.0/24 for labs is an example of:
items.why: Splitting an address space into smaller ranges is subnetting.

items.stem: Traffic between the staff VLAN and the server VLAN passes through a firewall that allows only required ports. What does this add?
items.why: Inter-zone filtering enforces policy between segments.

topics.title: Protecting Networks: Firewalls
topics.hook: A firewall has two rules. Rule 1: allow TCP 80 from anywhere. Rule 2: deny all traffic from 203.0.113.0/24. A web request arrives from 203.0.113.50. Does it get in?
concept: Firewalls filter traffic using rules in an access control list (ACL). Each rule matches on fields such as direction (inbound/outbound), source and destination IP, protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP), and port, then permits or denies. Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins; an implicit deny at the end blocks anything not explicitly allowed. Rule order therefore changes outcomes.

Stateless firewalls check each packet in isolation. Stateful firewalls (dynamic packet filtering) track connections, so replies to allowed outbound requests are let back in automatically. Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) add application awareness, intrusion prevention, and deeper inspection.

Placement: a network firewall sits at the boundary between zones, such as internet to DMZ and DMZ to internal. Common ports: 22 SSH, 23 Telnet (insecure), 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP.
terms: Ordered list of rules that permit or deny traffic.
Processing stops at the first rule that matches a packet.
Default rule blocking traffic not explicitly permitted.
Evaluates each packet alone, without connection context.
Tracks connection state; allows related return traffic.
Firewall adding application awareness and intrusion prevention.
Number identifying a service (e.g., 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH).

compare.title: Firewall types
rows: Per-packet, fast, needs explicit return rules

traps: Put specific deny rules above broad allow rules, or the allow matches first.
A rule allowing port 22 from ALL exposes SSH to the whole internet.

items.stem: ACL: Rule 1 Allow inbound TCP 443 from ANY. Rule 2 Deny inbound ANY from 198.51.100.0/24. A request to TCP 443 arrives from 198.51.100.7. What happens?
opts: Allowed only if Rule 2 is removed
items.why: First match wins: Rule 1 matches, so Rule 2 is never evaluated.

items.stem: To block 198.51.100.0/24 from the HTTPS server in the ACL above, what is the BEST fix?
opts: Move the deny rule above the allow rule
items.why: The specific deny must come before the broad allow.

items.stem: Which firewall automatically allows return traffic for a connection initiated from inside?
items.why: Stateful firewalls track sessions and permit related replies.

items.stem: An ACL contains 'Allow inbound TCP 23 from ANY.' What is the MAIN risk?
opts: Telnet is exposed to the internet and sends credentials in cleartext
items.why: Port 23 is Telnet, unencrypted remote login.

items.stem: A firewall identifies that traffic on port 443 is actually a file-sharing app and blocks it. Which type is it?
items.why: Application awareness is an NGFW feature.

items.stem: Where should a firewall be placed to protect internal servers if the public web server is compromised?
opts: Between the DMZ and the internal network
Between the printer and its cable
items.why: An inner firewall filters traffic from the DMZ to the internal network.

items.stem: An admin needs SSH access to a server only from the IT subnet 10.0.5.0/24. Which rule is BEST?
opts: Allow inbound TCP 22 from 10.0.5.0/24; everything else falls to implicit deny
items.why: Least-privilege rule: correct port, protocol, and narrow source.

items.stem: A packet matches no rule in an ACL that ends with an implicit deny. What happens?
opts: It is sent to the DMZ
items.why: Traffic not explicitly permitted is denied.

topics.title: Detecting Network Attacks
topics.hook: At 14:03 ICMP traffic to the web server jumps 4,000% and the switch shows two different MAC addresses claiming the gateway's IP. Which logs do you open, and what do you conclude?
concept: Network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) monitor traffic and alert; network intrusion prevention systems (NIPS) sit inline and can block. A SIEM (security information and event management) collects logs from firewalls, IDS/IPS, switches, routers, and servers, correlates them, and raises alerts.

Signature-based detection matches known attack patterns: accurate for known threats, blind to new ones. Anomaly-based detection compares activity to a baseline of normal behavior: it can catch novel attacks but produces more false positives. Hybrid systems combine both. AI and probabilistic thresholds help decide when deviation is significant.

Evidence to look for: spikes in ICMP (smurf, DoS), duplicate MAC entries for one IP in ARP tables (ARP poisoning), unknown SSIDs or radio noise (rogue AP, jamming), and repeated denied connections across ports (scanning). Tuning matters: too sensitive causes alert fatigue; too lax causes false negatives.
terms: Monitors network traffic and alerts on suspicious activity.
Inline system that can block suspicious traffic.
Central platform aggregating and correlating logs for alerts.
Detection by matching known attack patterns.
Detection by deviation from a normal baseline.
Measured normal behavior used for comparison.
Analysts ignoring alerts due to overwhelming volume.
traps: An IDS detects; an IPS can also prevent. Don't swap them.
A SIEM doesn't block traffic by itself. It correlates and alerts.

items.stem: The gateway's ARP table shows the router's IP mapped to two different MAC addresses within minutes. Which attack is MOST likely?
items.why: Conflicting MAC entries for one IP is a classic ARP poisoning indicator.

items.stem: Which system can automatically block malicious traffic in real time?
items.why: An IPS is inline and can drop traffic.

items.stem: A brand-new attack with no published signature hits the network. Which detection method is MOST likely to catch it?
items.why: Anomaly detection can flag unknown behavior that deviates from baseline.

items.stem: Which tool aggregates logs from firewalls, servers, and IDS devices into one place for correlation?
items.why: A SIEM centralizes and correlates logs.

items.stem: A firewall log shows one external IP attempting connections to ports 21, 22, 23, 25, 80, 443, 3389 within two seconds, all denied. What is this?
items.why: Rapid attempts across many ports is scanning.

items.stem: After making the IDS more sensitive, the team receives 10x more alerts, mostly harmless. What is the MAIN risk?
opts: Alert fatigue causing real attacks to be missed
items.why: Excessive false positives reduce attention to true positives.

items.stem: Monitoring shows a sudden flood of ICMP echo replies to the web server from many internal hosts at once. Which attack fits BEST?
items.why: Many hosts replying with ICMP to one target suggests broadcast amplification.

items.stem: An IDS fails to alert on an attack that actually occurred. This is a:
items.why: A missed real attack is a false negative.
